sections.title: A convex function lies above its tangent plane
sections.intro: This first lemma needs a real inner-product space but does not yet need completeness. Its derivative is the continuous linear map \lean{fderiv}; a gradient will be introduced later. We reduce the vector-space inequality to the familiar secant-slope inequality for a convex real function.

blocks.title: Read the statement and identify the goal
blocks.explanation: The implicit parameter \lean{f} is a function $H\to\R$. The named hypothesis \lean{hf} states convexity on the universal set, and \lean{hdiff} states differentiability at every point. The explicit points are \lean{x} and \lean{y}. The expression \lean{fderiv} applied to $y-x$ means $Df(x)[y-x]$; it is a real number. After \lean{:= by}, Lean asks us to prove\[ f(x)+Df(x)[y-x]\le f(y). \] The notation \lean{lemma} introduces a proved result, and braces mark parameters that Lean can infer when the result is used.

blocks.title: Restrict to an affine line
blocks.explanation: The local definition \lean{line} is the affine map $\ell(t)=t(y-x)+x$. Its type records that it is affine over $\R$. The new hypothesis \lean{hc} states that $f\circ\ell$ is convex on all of $\R$. The library method \lean{hf.comp_affineMap line} gives exactly the preservation of convexity under an affine restriction. The tactic \lean{simpa [line] using} simplifies the library statement, including the universal-set preimage, and unfolds the local definition enough to match the stated type. The original vector-space goal stays open; \lean{have} adds this scalar convexity fact to the context.

blocks.title: Differentiate the affine line
blocks.explanation: The hypothesis \lean{hl} will express $\ell'(0)=y-x$. The tactic \lean{change} replaces the affine-map notation by its definition, so its subgoal becomes a derivative statement for $t\mapsto t\mathbin{\cdot}(y-x)+x$. The library fact \lean{hasDerivAt_id} differentiates $t\mapsto t$ with derivative $1$. The method \lean{smul_const} multiplies that derivative by the fixed vector $y-x$, and \lean{add_const} adds $x$ without changing the derivative. The final \lean{simpa} removes $1\mathbin{\cdot}(y-x)$ and other definitional notation. We now have\[ \lean{hl}:\quad \ell'(0)=y-x. \] Here a scalar derivative may take values in $H$, so \lean{HasDerivAt} applies to this vector-valued line.

blocks.title: Use the chain rule and the convex secant inequality
blocks.explanation: From \lean{hdiff x}, the method \lean{hasFDerivAt} produces the derivative of $f$ at $x$. The method \lean{comp_hasDerivAt_of_eq} composes it with \lean{hl}; its final equality subgoal is $x=\ell(0)$, discharged by \lean{simp [line]}. Thus \lean{hd} states\[ (f\circ\ell)'(0)=Df(x)[y-x]. \] The next \lean{have} applies \lean{hc.le_slope_of_hasDerivAt}. The two \lean{Set.mem_univ} arguments certify that $0$ and $1$ belong to the convexity domain; \lean{zero_lt_one} supplies $0<1$; and \lean{hd} supplies the derivative. The resulting \lean{hs} is\[ Df(x)[y-x]\le \frac{(f\circ\ell)(1)-(f\circ\ell)(0)}{1-0}. \]

blocks.title: Simplify the slope and finish the linear rearrangement
blocks.explanation: The phrase \lean{simp only} uses just the listed rewrite facts. The modifier \lean{at hs} changes the hypothesis rather than the goal. The rules expand the slope and composition, evaluate $\ell(1)=y$ and $\ell(0)=x$, and simplify $1-0$ and division by $1$. Afterward,\[ \lean{hs}:\quad Df(x)[y-x]\le f(y)-f(x). \] Adding $f(x)$ to both sides is the remaining argument. The tactic \lean{linarith} checks this linear combination of inequalities and proves the original goal. No approximation or additional mathematical hypothesis is introduced by the tactic.

sections.title: Strong convexity gives the quadratic tangent model
sections.intro: The strong-convexity convention is the one used by Mathlib: subtracting $(m/2)\norm{x}^{2}$ produces a convex function. This lemma is valid for every real $m$; positivity of $m$ is imposed only in later conclusions. Completeness is now required to represent the derivative by the actual Mathlib gradient.

blocks.title: State the strong first-order inequality
Adjust the function and compute its derivative
blocks.explanation: The definition \lean{g} sets $g(v)=f(v)-(m/2)\norm{v}^{2}$. The library equivalence \lean{strongConvexOn_iff_convex} has strong convexity on its left and convexity of this adjusted function on its right. Its \lean{.mp} method uses the forward implication, sending \lean{hsc} to the new convexity hypothesis \lean{hc}. The family \lean{hg} gives a derivative at each $v$. The map \lean{innerSL} sends a direction $w$ to $\ip{v}{w}$, and \lean{hasStrictFDerivAt_norm_sq} gives the derivative $w\mapsto2\ip{v}{w}$ of the squared norm. The method \lean{const_mul} multiplies by $m/2$, while \lean{.sub} subtracts that derivative from the derivative of $f$. Hence\[ Dg(v)[w]=Df(v)[w]-\frac m2\bigl(2\ip{v}{w}\bigr). \] The coercions and scalar multiplications in the Lean expression are operations on continuous linear maps.

blocks.title: Apply the convex tangent lemma and expand its derivative
blocks.explanation:
The method \lean{(hg v).differentiableAt} forgets the particular derivative while retaining differentiability, so \lean{hgd} makes \lean{convex_first_order} applicable to $g$. The resulting \lean{hxy} initially says $g(x)+Dg(x)[y-x]\le g(y)$. The rewrite \lean{rw [(hg x).fderiv] at hxy} replaces the automatically defined derivative of $g$ by the explicit derivative certified by \lean{hg x}. The listed simplifications unfold $g$, evaluate sums and scalar multiples of linear maps, and use \lean{inner_gradient_left} backwards to turn $Df(x)[\cdot]$ into an inner product. They also expand inner products of differences. In ordinary notation the resulting hypothesis is\[ egin{aligned} f(x)- rac m2
orm{x}^{2}&+\ip{
abla f(x)}{y}-\ip{
abla f(x)}{x}\ &- rac m2\Bigl((\ip{x}{y}-
orm{x}^{2})+(\ip{x}{y}-
orm{x}^{2})\Bigr) \le f(y)- rac m2
orm{y}^{2}. \end{aligned}\] The \lean{two_smul} and \lean{add_apply} rules explain why the doubled inner-product term appears as a sum in this normalization.

blocks.title: Compare the expanded hypothesis with the expanded goal

sections.title: Strong monotonicity and the lower objective gap
sections.intro: The next two consequences use the strong first-order inequality directly. Strong monotonicity will construct a stationary point using a small auxiliary step. The lower objective gap will later convert decay of function values into decay of distance.

blocks.title: The strong-monotonicity goal
blocks.explanation:
The hypotheses \lean{hdiff} and \lean{hsc} have the same meaning as before, and the points $x,y$ are explicit. The goal is\[ m
orm{x-y}^{2}\le\ip{
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)}{x-y}. \] This compares the difference of gradients with the displacement. It is a lower bound on the inner product, rather than a bound on the gradient norm.

blocks.title: Write the tangent bounds in both directions
Add the two inequalities and cancel the function values
A stationary point gives the quadratic lower gap
blocks.explanation:
The implicit reference point \lean{z} comes with \lean{hz}, the equation $
abla f(z)=0$. Apply \lean{strong_first_order} with base point $z$ and target point $x$, obtaining\[ f(z)+\ip{
abla f(z)}{x-z}+ rac m2
orm{x-z}^{2}\le f(x). \] The rewrite \lean{rw [hz, inner_zero_left, add_zero] at h} replaces the gradient by zero, evaluates its inner product, and removes the zero summand. The remaining hypothesis is $f(z)+(m/2)
orm{x-z}^{2}\le f(x)$. The tactic \lean{linarith} subtracts $f(z)$ and proves\[  rac m2
orm{x-z}^{2}\le f(x)-f(z). \] The lemma itself does not assume $m>0$; when positivity is available, its left side is nonnegative and proves that $z$ minimizes $f$ globally.

sections.title: The gradient controls the objective gap
sections.intro: This upper gap bound is the completed-square form of strong convexity. It requires $m>0$ but accepts any reference point $z$. At a minimizer it becomes the Polyak--\L{}ojasiewicz inequality used in the descent proof.

blocks.title: Read the upper-gap statement
blocks.explanation: The new hypothesis \lean{hm} is $0<m$. The goal is\[ f(x)-f(z)\le\frac{\norm{\nabla f(x)}^{2}}{2m}. \] There is no \lean{hz} hypothesis and no assertion that $z$ minimizes $f$. This greater generality is intentional: the strong tangent model at $x$ is enough to bound its difference from any value $f(z)$. Later the actual minimizer supplies a nonnegative gap as well.

blocks.title: Use the signed Cauchy--Schwarz bound
Complete the square and discharge the division goal
blocks.explanation: The method \lean{hgap.trans} is transitivity with the established intermediate upper bound $B=as-(m/2)s^{2}$. Applying it replaces the original goal by $B\le a^{2}/(2m)$. The tactic \lean{positivity} proves $2m>0$ from \lean{hm}. For a positive denominator, \lean{le_div_iff} (with the subscript-$0$ suffix shown in the listing) is the equivalence $B\le a^{2}/(2m)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ B(2m)\le a^{2}$. The code uses its \lean{.2}, the implication from the multiplied inequality to the desired divided inequality, leaving\[ 2m\left(as-\frac m2s^{2}\right)\le a^{2}. \] Finally \lean{sq_nonneg} supplies\[ (ms-a)^{2}=m^{2}s^{2}-2mas+a^{2}\ge0. \] Rearranging gives $2mas-m^{2}s^{2}\le a^{2}$, exactly the remaining goal. The final \lean{nlinarith} expands the square and performs this rearrangement. Equivalently, the resulting bound can be multiplied by $2m>0$ to obtain $2m(f(x)-f(z))\le\norm{\nabla f(x)}^{2}$.

sections.title: Construct a stationary point with an auxiliary contraction
sections.intro: The file \lean{Minimizer.lean} imports the first-order lemmas and the step estimates. Existence does not assume a minimizer or finite dimensionality. It chooses a small gradient step and invokes the Banach fixed-point theorem on the complete space. The local Lean variable is printed as $\alpha$ in the listing; we denote it by $\beta$ here to distinguish this auxiliary choice from the user-selected step $\alpha$ in the convergence theorem.

blocks.title: Existence is a conclusion
blocks.explanation: The hypotheses \lean{hdiff}, \lean{hsc}, and \lean{hLip} give global differentiability, $m$-strong convexity, and an actual $L$-Lipschitz gradient. The constant $L$ has nonnegative-real type; \lean{hm} says $m>0$. Unlike the eventual convergence theorem, this existence result needs neither a prescribed step nor $L>0$. Its goal is an existential statement:\[ \exists z\in H,\qquad \nabla f(z)=0. \] The proof must supply both a point and a proof of its stationarity. Completeness is already present in the file's variable assumptions.

blocks.title: Choose the auxiliary step and prove it is positive
blocks.explanation: The local definition in the listing sets the auxiliary number\[ \beta=\frac{m}{L^{2}+m^{2}}. \] Although its Lean name is the same Greek letter used for the iteration step elsewhere, it is local to this theorem. It does not constrain the step chosen in \lean{gradient_descent_converges}. The fact \lean{hden} states $L^{2}+m^{2}>0$: squares are nonnegative and $m^{2}>0$ follows from \lean{hm}. The tactic \lean{positivity} assembles these facts. The library theorem \lean{div_pos hm hden} then proves the named positivity fact $\beta>0$. Thus both the numerator and denominator are certified positive before division is used.

blocks.title: Verify the contraction step restriction by explicit algebra
blocks.explanation: The subgoal \lean{hsmall} is $\beta L^{2}<2m$. The tactic \lean{dsimp} unfolds the local step definition. The first rewrite puts $(m/(L^{2}+m^{2}))L^{2}$ into the form $mL^{2}/(L^{2}+m^{2})$; the second uses the certified positive denominator \lean{hden} to turn the strict division inequality into\[ mL^{2}<2m(L^{2}+m^{2}). \] The difference between right and left is $mL^{2}+2m^{3}$. We have $L^{2}\ge0$ from \lean{sq_nonneg}, $m>0$ from \lean{hm}, and $m^{3}=m\cdot m^{2}>0$ from \lean{mul_pos hm (sq_pos_of_pos hm)}. Hence the difference is positive. The final \lean{nlinarith} verifies this polynomial argument. These rewrites use positivity explicitly, so the strict inequality direction is preserved.

blocks.title: Obtain a Banach fixed point
blocks.explanation:
The theorem \lean{contracting_gradient_step} is applied to the vector field $g=
abla f$, the parameters $m, eta,L$, the two step facts, strong monotonicity, and \lean{hLip}. Thus \lean{hc} says that\[ T_ eta(x)=x- eta
abla f(x) \] is a contraction with coefficient $q=\sqrt{1-2 eta m+ eta^{2}L^{2}}<1$, using the total real square-root convention proved in the step file. The expression \lean{strong_gradient_monotone hdiff hsc} supplies the required inequality for all pairs of points without naming those points again. The command \lean{obtain} destructures the existential conclusion of \lean{hc.exists_fixedPoint}. The start is $0\in H$; \lean{edist_ne_top} certifies finite extended distance in a normed space. We retain the fixed point \lean{z} and its fixed-point fact \lean{hz}, discarding the library's additional conclusions with the underscore. The next \lean{have} presents that fact explicitly as\[ \lean{hz'}:\quad z- eta
abla f(z)=z. \]

blocks.title: Turn the fixed-point equation into stationarity
blocks.explanation:
The equivalence \lean{sub_eq_self} says that $z-v=z$ is equivalent to $v=0$. Its \lean{.mp} uses the forward direction on \lean{hz'}, proving the new fact\[ \lean{hzero}:\quad  eta
abla f(z)=0. \] The equivalence \lean{smul_eq_zero} turns this scalar-product equation into the disjunction $ eta=0$ or $
abla f(z)=0$; again \lean{.mp} is the forward direction. The proof \lean{ne_of_gt} obtained from positivity of $ eta$ rules out the left disjunct. The method \lean{resolve_left} therefore returns $
abla f(z)=0$. Finally \lean{exact} supplies the existential pair consisting of $z$ and that proof. This completes attainment through the fixed-point theorem, rather than assuming that a minimum already exists.

sections.title: Stationarity implies global minimality and uniqueness
sections.intro: The lower gap lemma alone proves both properties. No converse theorem asserting that every minimizer is stationary is needed: any second global minimizer must coincide with the stationary point by the positive quadratic lower bound.

blocks.title: Split the conjunction into two proof goals
blocks.explanation: The hypothesis \lean{hz} says $\nabla f(z)=0$ and \lean{hm} says $m>0$. The conclusion has two parts:\[ (\forall x\in H,\ f(z)\le f(x))\quad\text{and}\quad (\forall y\in H,\ (\forall x\in H,\ f(y)\le f(x))\Rightarrow y=z). \] The first is global minimality; the second is uniqueness among all global minimizers. The tactic \lean{constructor} applies the introduction rule for a conjunction and creates two goals. The two indented bullet branches in the remaining proof solve them separately.

blocks.title: Prove global minimality from a nonnegative lower gap
blocks.explanation: The command \lean{intro x} fixes an arbitrary point for the universal quantifier in the first goal. The fact \lean{h} is\[ \frac m2\norm{x-z}^{2}\le f(x)-f(z). \] The new fact \lean{hn}, established by \lean{positivity}, says its left side is nonnegative, using $m>0$ and the nonnegative square. Combining the two inequalities gives $0\le f(x)-f(z)$, equivalently $f(z)\le f(x)$. The tactic \lean{linarith} checks that rearrangement and closes the first branch. The proof has made no special choice of $x$, so global minimality follows.

blocks.title: Force any other minimizer to have zero squared distance
blocks.explanation: In the second branch, \lean{intro y hy} fixes another point $y$ and assumes its global minimality \lean{hy}. The lower gap gives \lean{h}, and specializing \lean{hy} at $z$ gives \lean{hmin}: $f(y)\le f(z)$. Let $S=\norm{y-z}^{2}$. Inside the nested proof of \lean{hsq}, \lean{sq_nonneg} supplies \lean{hnonneg}: $S\ge0$. The inequalities now read\[ 0\le S,\qquad \frac m2S\le f(y)-f(z)\le0,\qquad m>0. \] If $S$ were positive, then $(m/2)S$ would be positive and could not be bounded above by zero. Therefore $S=0$. The tactic \lean{nlinarith} verifies this consequence using the positive parameter $m$ and the polynomial inequalities. This is why strict positivity of the strong-convexity constant is needed for uniqueness.

blocks.title: Convert zero norm into equality of points
blocks.explanation: The equivalence \lean{sq_eq_zero_iff} sends \lean{hsq}, the equation $\norm{y-z}^{2}=0$, to \lean{hn}: $\norm{y-z}=0$ through its forward \lean{.mp} direction. The inner application \lean{norm_eq_zero.mp hn} then proves $y-z=0$. The outer application \lean{sub_eq_zero.mp} turns that equation into $y=z$. Thus the final \lean{exact} gives the required equality, closes the uniqueness branch, and completes the conjunction.

sections.title: Package the unique-minimizer theorem
sections.intro: This final result combines the construction of a stationary point with the two preceding consequences. The notation for unique existence records a witness, its property, and uniqueness of every other witness satisfying the same property.

blocks.title: Understand the unique-existence goal
blocks.explanation: The function assumptions are the same as those of \lean{exists_stationary}: differentiability, $m$-strong convexity with $m>0$, and a globally $L$-Lipschitz gradient. The conclusion\[ \exists! z\in H,\qquad \forall x\in H,\ f(z)\le f(x) \] uses Lean's unique-existence notation. Expanding that notation, we must provide one $z$, prove global minimality at $z$, and prove that any point with global minimality equals $z$. It does not require a preselected candidate minimizer.

blocks.title: Assemble the witness and its two properties
blocks.explanation: The first \lean{obtain} applies \lean{exists_stationary} and names both the resulting witness \lean{z} and its stationarity proof \lean{hz}. The second applies \lean{stationary_unique_minimizer}; destructuring its conjunction names the two proofs \lean{hmin} and \lean{huniq}. They have exactly the minimality and uniqueness types required by the expanded unique-existence goal. The final triple supplied by \lean{exact} consists of the witness, the proof of its property, and the proof of uniqueness. This assembly changes no assumptions and introduces no new analytic argument.
